section_summary: This section documents the unfolding events of the February 26 Incident (1936 military coup) in Tokyo and the international diplomatic reactions to it between February 26 and March 2, 1936. Reports from American diplomatic posts in Tokyo, Peiping, Nanking, Moscow, and Paris trace the assassinations of government leaders, the imposition of martial law, the standoff with insurgent officers, the miraculous survival of Prime Minister Okada, and the eventual surrender of the mutineers without widespread fighting. State Department analyses, together with Chinese and Soviet diplomatic assessments, examine the internal political causes of the rebellion and express serious concern over its potential impact on Japanese militarism, Sino-Japanese relations, and stability throughout the Far East.

subfiles.about: A preliminary Department of State analysis of the military coup in Tokyo, its casualties, background causes, and potential political trajectory.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck reviews initial telegrams from Tokyo reporting the February 26 army uprising aimed at assassinating political leaders and moderate officials. He notes the reported deaths of the Prime Minister, Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal, and Inspector General of Military Education, as well as attacks on other ministers. Hornbeck attributes the coup to reactionary-radical 'Fascist' younger officers seeking direct imperial rule and purification of government following factional friction in the army. He concludes that the coup represents another attempt by military elements to make the armed forces completely authoritative in state affairs.
subfiles.title: The Military Coup in Tokyo

subfiles.about: A transmittal note drawing the Secretary of State's attention to Japanese thought and the global threat posed by a militant Japan.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck urges Secretary of State Hull to examine an accompanying memorandum that sheds light on Japanese psychology. He expresses concern that few in the United States adequately realize the global danger posed by a militant Japan on the move. Hornbeck laments that more Americans do not possess sufficient information to understand these inevitable developments.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Secretary of State regarding Japanese Psychology and Militancy

subfiles.about: Ambassador Bullitt reports information received from Japanese Ambassador Ota concerning the coup in Tokyo and possible candidates for Prime Minister.
subfiles.from: William C. Bullitt, American Ambassador to the Soviet Union (Moscow)
subfiles.summary: Japanese Ambassador Ota informs Bullitt of a message from Foreign Minister Hirota detailing the mutiny of the First Division's Third Regiment and the murders of Admiral Okada, Finance Minister Takahashi, and Viscount Saito, along with Makino's narrow escape. A state of danger of war short of martial law was declared, while quiet prevailed in Tokyo and no Foreign Office personnel were harmed. Ota predicted extreme difficulty in selecting a new Prime Minister, suggesting General Araki or General Ugaki as potential appointees.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 67 from Moscow regarding Tokyo Coup Reports

subfiles.about: Consul Grummon inquires whether the Department wants locally available information amid reports of communications disruptions in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Stuart K. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.summary: The American Consulate at Dairen reports alarming rumors concerning the situation in Tokyo and alleged suspension of all communications from Japan. Consul Grummon asks whether the State Department desires the consulate to transmit information available locally in Dairen.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Dairen regarding Alarming Reports from Tokyo

subfiles.about: The State Department instructs the Dairen consulate that Tokyo communications remain open and to report only locally originating information.
subfiles.from: Department of State (Cordell Hull)
subfiles.summary: Responding to Grummon's inquiry, the Department of State informs the Dairen Consulate that communications between Washington and the Embassy in Tokyo are not interrupted. Grummon is directed to report only information originating locally.
subfiles.title: Telegram to Dairen regarding Communications with Tokyo

subfiles.about: Lockhart reports rumors from Shanghai regarding the Tokyo coup and live ammunition issued to troops departing for Manchuria.
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, American Embassy Counselor at Peiping
subfiles.summary: Lockhart notes Japanese efforts to prevent telegraphic reports about Tokyo events while local Japanese officials acknowledge a serious situation. Unconfirmed Shanghai reports state that the First Division's Third Regiment took advantage of live ammunition issued prior to departure for Manchuria to assassinate political leaders and occupy government buildings.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 90 from Peiping regarding Coup Reports and Troop Movements

subfiles.about: The State Department informs the Peiping Embassy that communications with Tokyo have not been interrupted.
subfiles.from: Department of State (Cordell Hull)
subfiles.summary: In reference to Peiping's telegram No. 90, the State Department advises Lockhart that communication between the Tokyo Embassy and the Department is not interrupted.
subfiles.title: Telegram to Peiping regarding Communications with Tokyo

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the appointment of Home Minister Goto as acting Premier and confirms Count Makino is unharmed.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that an extra edition of the Tokyo Nichi Nichi announced Home Minister Goto's appointment as temporary acting Premier. Furthermore, the Embassy learned from a reliable informant who spoke directly with Count Makino that Makino was neither killed nor wounded during the uprising.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 39 from Tokyo regarding Acting Premier and Makino's Safety

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports that a Department message was transmitted to Foreign Minister Hirota's secretary while Hirota attended Palace conferences.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Referring to the Department's telegram No. 25, Grew states that Foreign Minister Hirota was expected to spend the entire day in conferences at the Imperial Palace. Consequently, Grew delivered the text of the message to Hirota's secretary, who undertook to hand it directly to the Minister.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 40 from Tokyo regarding Delivery of Message to Hirota

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew details confirmed assassinations, the declaration of martial law, financial market conditions, and delicate negotiations with the insurgents.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Grew confirms the deaths of Premier Okada, Admiral Saito, General Watanabe, and Finance Minister Takahashi, while Admiral Suzuki was severely wounded and Prince Saionji remained safe. Martial law was declared under General Kashii to establish legal control, restrict movement, and negotiate with the rebel soldiers concentrated at the Premier's official residence. The insurgents demanded a military dictatorship, which the Palace Council rejected, and discussions continue regarding a compromise premier such as Araki, Higashikuni, or Yamamoto. Military authorities are avoiding armed assault to prevent civilian casualties and avoid creating martyrs among the popular young officers. This file unit also includes a complete duplicate copy of the multi-section telegram.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 41 from Tokyo regarding Casualties, Martial Law, and Insurgent Negotiations

subfiles.about: Ambassador Johnson transmits Chinese official views, noting Foreign Minister Chang Chun's expectation of a temporary reduction in Japanese external pressure.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Ambassador to China (Nanking)
subfiles.summary: Johnson reports that Chinese officials initially feared the Tokyo coup would lead to intensified Japanese aggression under military control. However, Chinese Foreign Minister Chang Chun privately opined that Japanese chauvinistic pressure on China would temporarily subside while Japan focused on resolving domestic instability. Chang expressed concern over the damage to Japan's governance, noting that the military clique systematically eliminated the Emperor's trusted moderate advisers to gain exclusive control over the Throne. The document includes the State Department's confidential paraphrase sheet.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 42 from Nanking regarding Chinese Official Reactions to the Tokyo Coup

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports an evening ultimatum to the insurgents, an apparent temporary compromise, and troop movements around the heavily guarded Embassy.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Grew informs Washington that the Japanese government delivered an ultimatum to the insurgents at 8 p.m. on February 27, resulting in an undisclosed temporary compromise. Widespread rumors of impending military action circulated due to movements of troops and machine guns across Tokyo. Grew reports no immediate danger to American interests and notes that loyal government troops heavily guard the Embassy. The text is accompanied by the official State Department paraphrase.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 43 from Tokyo regarding Government Ultimatum and Embassy Security

subfiles.about: Ambassador Straus summarizes French political and parliamentary analyses concerning the potential international repercussions of the Tokyo coup.
subfiles.from: Jesse I. Straus, American Ambassador to France (Paris)
subfiles.summary: Straus reports that French commentators initially viewed the coup as an ultra-nationalist movement driven by radical socialistic economic demands, but broader concerns quickly emerged. A majority of political observers in Paris fear the coup may serve as a prelude to Japanese military action against China and Soviet Russia. In the French Parliament, debates centered on whether the Franco-Soviet Pact could draw France into Far Eastern conflicts, though deputies emphasized its terms exclude Russia's eastern frontier unless a conflict widened.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 147 from Paris regarding French Press and Parliamentary Opinion

subfiles.about: Ambassador Bullitt reports Soviet Assistant Commissar Stomonyakov's intelligence and fears of Japanese expansion into North China and Outer Mongolia.
subfiles.from: William C. Bullitt, American Ambassador to the Soviet Union (Moscow)
subfiles.summary: Soviet Assistant Commissar Boris Stomonyakov shared reports that mutineers still occupied the War Ministry and police headquarters, while the Japanese cabinet remained sheltered in the Imperial Palace. Stomonyakov warned that General Masaki might be behind the mutiny and labeled him the most dangerous militarist, while viewing Prince Chichibu's summons to Tokyo as an ominous sign. He anticipated that the Japanese Army would launch an immediate advance against China or Outer Mongolia to secure an easy victory for public consumption, while avoiding a direct clash with the Soviet Union.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 71 from Moscow regarding Soviet Assessments of Mutiny and Foreign Policy

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports government preparations for an attack on rebel strongholds and declines an army offer to evacuate Embassy personnel.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Grew reports government forces concentrating tanks near the British Embassy in apparent preparation for an assault on the Premier's residence and the Sanno Hotel. A martial law staff officer offered to transfer the American Embassy staff to the military academy for safety against stray bullets, but Grew declined, having instituted precautionary measures and deemed the Embassy's defenses adequate. He indicates that an ultimatum to the insurgents is likely set to expire during the day.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 44 from Tokyo regarding Troop Deployments and Embassy Evacuation Offer

subfiles.about: The State Department commends Ambassador Grew and staff for their handling of the crisis and authorizes funds for emergency protection.
subfiles.from: Department of State (Wilbur J. Carr / Cordell Hull)
subfiles.summary: Responding to telegram No. 44, the Department expresses high appreciation for the sense of duty and timely reporting demonstrated by Grew and his staff. Full confidence is placed in Grew's discretion regarding whether to evacuate personnel from the danger zone, warning against unnecessary risks. The Department confirms that special allowances will be granted upon request should movements of personnel or property require expenditures.
subfiles.title: Telegram to Tokyo Commending Embassy Conduct and Authorizing Expenditures

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports peaceful negotiations following an imperial order, naval fleet movements, and press speculation on a national cabinet.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that tension relaxed without armed combat after the First Division Commander delivered an imperial order directing the insurgents to return to barracks. Takahashi's death was officially confirmed, precipitating large bank withdrawals, while communications censorship was re-tightened after temporary lifting. Naval vessels from Yokosuka, including the First Fleet, arrived in Tokyo Bay for guard duty, and vernacular newspapers advocated the formation of a strong national cabinet free from the influence of court cliques.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 45 from Tokyo regarding Standoff Negotiations and Naval Dispositions

subfiles.about: Ambassador Johnson transmits translations of Chinese newspaper editorials on the strategic implications of the Tokyo crisis.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Ambassador to China (Nanking)
subfiles.summary: Johnson transmits Reuters translations of editorials from major Chinese newspapers published in Shanghai, including the China Times, Lih Pao, Sin Wen Pao, and Shun Pao. The papers concur that the coup is far more consequential than the May 15, 1932 incident, marking the ascendancy of the military and the decline of the capitalist and peerage classes. They warn that a militarized Japanese government will seek foreign adventures in China to distract from domestic instability, urging the Chinese public to prepare for increased external pressure.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 43 from Nanking Transmitting Chinese Press Comment

subfiles.about: Ambassador Johnson reports assessments from high Chinese officials and the Soviet Ambassador predicting Japanese aggression against China rather than Russia.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Ambassador to China (Nanking)
subfiles.summary: Chinese officials consulted by Johnson believe the coup portends a more aggressive Japanese posture toward China and Russia, speculating on the likelihood of war between Japan and the USSR. The Soviet Ambassador in Nanking, however, argued that Japan will hesitate to confront fortified Soviet positions in Siberia and will instead exploit a weak and divided China, potentially reigniting Chinese civil war. The Soviet envoy characterized events in Japan as a natural fascist evolution leading to inflation and heightened military expenditures. A confidential paraphrase sheet is appended.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 44 from Nanking on Soviet and Chinese Strategic Appraisals

subfiles.about: A cross-reference sheet pointing to despatch No. 897 concerning a conversation between American and Japanese embassy officials in Istanbul.
subfiles.from: G. Howland Shaw, American Embassy in Turkey (Istanbul)
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note cross-references despatch No. 897 (filed under 711.94/1065) from Istanbul, Turkey, dated January 30, 1936. The underlying despatch records a memorandum of conversation between Walter S. Washington of the American Embassy and Mr. Saito of the Japanese Embassy regarding the internal political situation in Japan.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 897 from Turkey on Internal Situation in Japan

subfiles.about: Ambassador Bullitt reports Litvinov's briefings indicating government control in Tokyo, Saionji's firm advice, and Prince Konoe as likely Premier.
subfiles.from: William C. Bullitt, American Ambassador to the Soviet Union (Moscow)
subfiles.summary: Soviet Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinov informed Bullitt of reports from the Soviet Ambassador in Tokyo indicating loyal troops controlled the city and Prince Saionji had advised the Emperor to show no mercy to the mutineers. Litvinov stated that General Masaki had no chance of becoming Premier and that Prince Konoe was the likely choice, making the outlook brighter for the USSR by averting an extremist cabinet. Chinese Ambassador W. W. Yen added that increased Japanese pressure on China was unlikely for several weeks. The telegram is accompanied by an FE paraphrase sheet.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 73 from Moscow on Soviet Optimism and Cabinet Prospects

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the rebels' rejection of an imperial ultimatum, their demands, and impending military suppression at daybreak.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: A high-ranking Japanese informant informed Grew that the insurgents rejected an ultimatum from the Emperor delivered at 3 p.m. to disband, prompting the government to order an armed assault at daybreak on February 29. The insurgents demand the appointment of General Masaki as Prime Minister, transfer of zaibatsu wealth from Mitsui and Mitsubishi to the government, and the release of Colonel Aizawa. Radio announcements confirmed military steps against rebel forces in Kojimachi, and Grew observed troops deployed around the British and American Embassies preparing for heavy fighting. A confidential paraphrase sheet is attached.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 46 from Tokyo regarding Impending Military Action and Rebel Demands

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports for a press conference that excellent order was maintained in Tokyo and no Americans were molested.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Grew sends a brief message intended for use in the Department's press conference stating that excellent order prevailed throughout Tokyo during the incident. He confirms that no American citizens have suffered injury or molestation beyond minor inconveniences caused by official precautionary measures.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 50 from Tokyo regarding Safety of American Citizens

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew announces the full surrender of the revolting troops and restoration of normal conditions.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the official announcement that all revolting troops surrendered and that normal conditions would be restored in Tokyo at 4:10 on February 29. The subfile includes both the original incoming cable and the corrected copy amending the time of restoration from morning to afternoon.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 49 from Tokyo Announcing Surrender of Insurgent Troops

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew details the surrender of rebel contingents following radio appeals, airborne leaflets, and martial law blockades.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Grew expresses gratitude for the Department's message of support and describes protective measures at the Chancery residence where staff families are housed behind barricades. He recounts how radio broadcasts and airplane leaflets warned insurgent rank-and-file soldiers that they would be treated as traitors unless they obeyed the Emperor's command to return to barracks. By morning, roughly 300 soldiers from the Sanno Hotel area and smaller groups with machine guns surrendered, while naval ships withdrew toward Yokohama as the government patiently resolved the standoff without fighting.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 47 from Tokyo regarding Surrender Operations, Leaflets, and Broadcasts

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports ongoing surrenders of soldiers and the near evacuation of the Premier's residence without fighting.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that radio bulletins confirm over a hundred additional soldiers surrendered, leaving only a handful with the mutinous officers at the Premier's official residence. Street observations confirm small groups of privates continually giving themselves up without armed conflict, and authorities anticipate an imminent lifting of newspaper bans and communication curbs.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 48 from Tokyo on the Progress of Insurgent Evacuation

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports that Prime Minister Okada escaped assassination, having been hidden while his brother-in-law was mistakenly killed.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Baron Hayashi informs Grew that Premier Keisuke Okada survived unharmed after rebels mistakenly killed his look-alike brother-in-law, Colonel Denzo Matsuo, while Okada hid until safely reaching the Imperial Palace. Acting Premier Goto resigned immediately as Okada resumed the premiership to the Emperor's reported gratification. Grew suggests this dramatic outcome could provoke a nationwide public revulsion against the military and notes that 15 to 20 junior officers involved face suicide or prosecution. A paraphrase sheet is included.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 51 from Tokyo on the Dramatic Survival of Premier Okada

subfiles.about: Consul Merrill reports Yokohama remained completely quiet throughout the crisis with shipping and residents unharmed.
subfiles.from: Keith Merrill, American Consul at Yokohama
subfiles.summary: Merrill reports that Yokohama has experienced uninterrupted tranquility, with merchant shipping arriving and departing on schedule. No American residents were endangered, though several were temporarily unable to commute to Tokyo offices due to rail suspensions, and a staff member is recovering from surgery.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Yokohama on Local Tranquility and American Residents

subfiles.about: Lockhart transmits a report from the Mukden Consulate General assessing local reactions to the Tokyo crisis under tight military control.
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, American Embassy Counselor at Peiping
subfiles.summary: Lockhart conveys a telegram from Consul General Ballantine in Mukden noting that public reaction to the Tokyo crisis appears muted because of stringent press censorship and existing army control. Japanese residents guardedly express regret and hope moderate elements prevail, while Chinese officials voice anxiety over heightened tensions, and military headquarters conducts frequent conferences. A confidential paraphrase sheet is attached.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 99 from Peiping Transmitting Mukden Reactions

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the return of normal street conditions, Captain Nonaka's suicide, and the summary dismissal and arrest of rebel officers.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that although martial law remains in force, normal life has returned to Tokyo, street barricades have been dismantled, and regular police have replaced soldiers on patrol. An official announcement confirmed that Captain Nonaka committed suicide by seppuku, while the remaining officers were imprisoned and dishonorably dismissed from the army without trial, signaling an unusually rigorous punitive policy. Deliberations continue regarding the formation of a new cabinet and the selection of a Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 52 from Tokyo on Normalization, Arrests, and Disgrace of Rebel Officers

subfiles.about: Lockhart reviews editorials from Chinese and Japanese-controlled newspapers in Peiping examining the ideological roots of the coup.
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, American Embassy Counselor at Peiping
subfiles.summary: Lockhart summarizes press reactions in Peiping, contrasting independent Chinese papers with the Japanese-controlled Asia People's Voice. The latter justified the coup as a modernizing revolution stemming from election corruption, agrarian distress among young officers, the Minobe constitutional controversy, and the Okada cabinet's Minseito electoral victory. Independent papers like Ta Kung Pao, Shih Chieh Jih Pao, and Hua Pei Jih Pao expressed anxiety over regional stability, warning that the coup would damage Japan's global standing and accelerate an international arms race.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 98 from Peiping Reviewing Chinese Press Analyses

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports confidential assurances from the Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs regarding foreign policy, and thanks authorities for protection.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan (Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs Shigemitsu confidentially assured Grew that cabinet deliberations prioritize forming a government dedicated to maintaining and constructively improving relations with foreign powers. Grew notes that tangible proof must be awaited and that cabinet formation will require several days. Additionally, Grew sent a formal letter to Foreign Minister Hirota expressing gratitude for the effective protection provided to Embassy staff and premises during the uprising. A paraphrase sheet is included.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 53 from Tokyo on Cabinet Formation and Foreign Policy Intentions

subfiles.about: A preliminary ONI intelligence summary outlining reported assassinations, casualties, troop strengths, and naval command changes in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Office of Naval Intelligence, Navy Department
subfiles.summary: The Office of Naval Intelligence summarizes early reports from Tokyo indicating that a fascist faction of soldiers and sailors seized control of government facilities. The document lists confirmed deaths including Takahashi, Okada, Saito, and Watanabe, along with casualties among police guards and servants. It notes reports that Navy Minister Admiral Osumi assumed the premiership and that martial law was declared around government buildings.
subfiles.title: Office of Naval Intelligence Memorandum on Situation in Tokyo
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: A priority naval message from the Fourth Marines in Shanghai transmitting operational dispatch traffic regarding the Far Eastern crisis.
subfiles.from: Fourth Marines (Shanghai)
subfiles.summary: This priority naval radio communication sent by the Fourth Marines in Shanghai to the Commander-in-Chief, Asiatic Fleet, with information copies to COMYANGPAT and OPNAV, relays early intelligence communications received in Shanghai on February 26, 1936. The message was transmitted to the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs for monitoring.
subfiles.title: Naval Message from Fourth Marines Shanghai to Commander-in-Chief Asiatic Fleet

subfiles.about: A priority naval communication originating from the Fourth Marines in Shanghai regarding the Japanese situation.
subfiles.from: Fourth Marines, Shanghai
subfiles.summary: This priority naval dispatch originating from the Fourth Marines in Shanghai communicates priority message traffic to the Commander-in-Chief, Asiatic Fleet, and Chief of Naval Operations. It was routed through the Far Eastern Affairs division of the State Department.
subfiles.title: Naval Message from Fourth Marines Shanghai to Commander-in-Chief Asiatic Fleet

subfiles.about: A priority naval dispatch relayed to the Commander-in-Chief, Asiatic Fleet, and Chief of Naval Operations.
subfiles.from: Fourth Marines
subfiles.summary: The Fourth Marines transmit priority operational traffic to the Commander-in-Chief, Asiatic Fleet, and OPNAV, noting internal routing and coordination with Lieutenant Blackledge. The State Department Division of Far Eastern Affairs logged the dispatch on February 26, 1936.
subfiles.title: Naval Message from Fourth Marines to Commander-in-Chief Asiatic Fleet

subfiles.about: The U.S. Naval Attaché at Peiping reports unconfirmed press bulletins alleging the assassination of Japan's Premier, Home Minister, and Finance Minister.
subfiles.from: American Naval Attaché, Peiping (ALUSNA Peiping)
subfiles.summary: ALUSNA Peiping transmits restricted message No. 026 to OPNAV and CINCAF reporting unconfirmed press accounts that the Japanese Prime Minister, Home Minister, and Finance Minister were assassinated during an army coup in Tokyo. The dispatch was logged by the State Department code room on February 26, 1936.
subfiles.title: Naval Message No. 026 from ALUSNA Peiping on Tokyo Military Coup
subfiles.to: Office of the Chief of Naval Operations (OPNAV)

subfiles.about: A naval radio dispatch from the Fourth Marines in Shanghai transmitting traffic to the Asiatic Fleet and Chief of Naval Operations.
subfiles.from: Fourth Marines, Shanghai
subfiles.summary: This naval dispatch from the Fourth Marines in Shanghai routes priority radio group 266 to the Commander-in-Chief, Asiatic Fleet, with information copies to OPNAV and COMYANGPAT. The dispatch was received and recorded by the State Department's Division of Far Eastern Affairs.
subfiles.title: Naval Message from Fourth Marines Shanghai to Commander-in-Chief Asiatic Fleet
